doctrines.question: Is salvation found only through Jesus Christ?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition in the registry confesses that salvation is through Christ alone: there is no other name given among people by which anyone must be saved, and no other mediator between God and humanity. This is not a live dispute within the church; the genuinely contested questions are what becomes of those who never hear that name, addressed next, and how the other religions are to be assessed, addressed after that.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the first tier: a denial of it abandons the gospel itself.

open.todo: Confirm there is no daylight between this settled claim and the pluralist alternative sometimes proposed alongside it.

positions.label: Salvation in Christ alone
positions.hold: Salvation is found only in Jesus Christ, who alone is the one mediator between God and humanity and the name by which anyone must be saved.
positions.why: Peter tells the Sanhedrin there is salvation in no one else, and Paul names one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, without qualification or exception.
positions.vs: Treating the world's religions as equally valid paths to God alongside faith in Christ.

held_by.note: The Covenant says: "Jesus Christ, being himself the only God-Man, who gave himself as the only ransom for sinners, is the only mediator between God and people."
held_by.citation: Lausanne Covenant (1974), Article 3, 'The Uniqueness and Universality of Christ'

held_by.note: The statement says: "Man's only hope of redemption is through the shed blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God" (Article 5, The Salvation of Man — not Article 3, which is about Christ's deity rather than salvation's exclusivity).
held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 5

held_by.note: The statement says Christ arose “to validate that the way of salvation is through Him alone.”
held_by.citation: International Network of Churches, Statement of Faith (Declaration of Faith, February 2022), "Jesus: Our Saviour"

held_by.note: The confession calls Christ “the One Mediator, fully God, fully man, in whose Person is effected the reconciliation between God and man.”
held_by.citation: Baptist Faith and Message (2000), Article II.B
Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XVIII
Westminster Confession of Faith 10.4
Catechism of the Catholic Church, 846-848; Lumen Gentium 14

held_by.note: Decree 8 says: "our Lord Jesus Christ [is] the only mediator, and ... in giving Himself a ransom for all He hath through His own Blood made a reconciliation between God and man." The previous citation to Decree 1 (the Trinity) was the wrong decree.
held_by.citation: Confession of Dositheus, Synod of Jerusalem (1672), Decree 8

held_by.note: The Smalcald Articles say "there is none other name under heaven, given among men whereby we must be saved." Retargeted from Augsburg Confession, Article III-IV, which teach Christ's atonement and justification by faith but do not state the exclusivity claim this directly.
held_by.citation: Smalcald Articles (1537), Part II, Article 1, "The First and Chief Article"
Articles of Religion (1784), Article II

held_by.note: The confession says of Christ: “He is the Son of the living God, in whom alone consist all our hope, consolation, redemption, and salvation, which we neither may nor must seek in any other.”
held_by.citation: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), Article 4

held_by.note: The chapter states: "To be out of him, or not under his mediatorship or government, is to be... unpardoned, unjustified, unsanctified, unreconciled, and an alien from the family of God, lost in trespasses and sins."
held_by.citation: Alexander Campbell, The Christian System, 1839, 'Remission of Sins'

positions.learn_detail: This is the one claim in the domain every registered tradition confesses without exception; the disputes that follow it are about the unevangelised and about how to assess the other religions, never about this.

positions.label: Pluralism
positions.hold: The major world religions are independently valid human responses to the same divine reality, so that faith in Christ is one legitimate path among several rather than the sole way of salvation.
positions.why: The great religious traditions each produce transformed lives and call their adherents from self-centredness toward the divine, which is read as evidence that they are alternative, equally adequate responses to one ultimate reality.
positions.vs: Confining salvation to explicit faith in Jesus Christ as the one mediator between God and humanity.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether Christ is the only way to God or one of several. Hick's version treats "God made human" as metaphor; the Nicene Creed (381) confesses Jesus as true God.
Who: Pluralists such as John Hick and some liberal Protestant writers vs. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, which confess Christ as the only mediator.
At stake: Pluralists say a loving God is not limited to one path; the churches point to John 14:6.
positions.learn_detail: Pluralism is most associated with the philosopher John Hick and finds an institutional home in some liberal Protestant currents outside this registry's twelve traditions; it is not the confessional position of any tradition listed here, so held_by is left empty rather than assigned to a body that has not adopted it.

sources.label: John Hick, An Interpretation of Religion

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: Exclusivism — salvation comes through Christ alone; pluralism — the major religions are all valid paths to God; mediator — someone who stands between two sides, here God and people; creed — a short statement of core belief that churches share.
How it developed: From the first century Christians called Christ the only mediator (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). The creeds of the 4th and 5th centuries fixed who Christ is. In the 1970s the philosopher John Hick argued for pluralism.

doctrines.question: What becomes of those who die never having heard the gospel?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition here confesses that salvation is through Christ alone; the dispute is what that means for someone who never hears his name. Some hold that explicit faith in Christ is necessary and so the unevangelised are lost; others hold Christ's saving work can be applied to those who respond in faith to the light of God's revelation they do have, without ever hearing the gospel by name; others hold that death itself is not the last opportunity to hear; and a further position holds that God has so ordered history, by his knowledge of what every person would freely do in any circumstance, that no one who would have believed the gospel if they heard it ever in fact fails to hear it.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the third tier: it is a matter theologians within the same tradition may disagree over without dividing fellowship, but it is not peripheral to how missions itself is understood.

open.todo: Work out how Romans 2's language of those who do not have the law but do what the law requires relates to Romans 10's insistence that faith comes by hearing, and settle whether the Molinist account of God's providential ordering of who hears the gospel is the better resolution of that tension than inclusivism.

positions.label: Restrictivism
positions.hold: Explicit, conscious faith in Jesus Christ is necessary for salvation, so that those who die without ever hearing and believing the gospel are lost.
positions.why: Paul asks how anyone can call on the one they have not believed in, and how they can believe without hearing, and how they can hear without a preacher being sent, making explicit hearing and believing the ordinary means God has appointed.
positions.vs: Holding that saving faith can be exercised toward Christ by someone who has never heard of him, on the basis of the general revelation available to them.

held_by.note: The Confession says such persons "never truly come unto Christ, and therefore cannot be saved," and calls the claim that they may be saved otherwise "very pernicious, and to be detested."
held_by.citation: Westminster Confession of Faith 10.4

held_by.note: The Covenant says: "We recognize that everyone has some knowledge of God through his general revelation in nature. But we deny that this can save, for people suppress the truth by their unrighteousness."
held_by.citation: Lausanne Covenant (1974), Article 3, 'The Uniqueness and Universality of Christ'

positions.label: Inclusivism
positions.hold: Christ is the only saviour, but his atoning work can be applied to those who, without ever hearing the gospel, respond in sincere faith and love to God as he has made himself known to them through creation and conscience.
positions.why: Those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel of Christ but sincerely seek God, and try to do his will as they know it through the dictates of conscience, can achieve eternal salvation, since it is Christ who enlightens all who are willing to arrive at the truth.
positions.vs: Requiring explicit, conscious faith in the name of Jesus Christ as a condition of the salvation his death secured.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether someone who never hears of Jesus can be saved by Christ if they sincerely seek God through conscience and creation.
Who: Catholic teaching (Lumen Gentium 16), most Orthodox, Anglican teaching and some Methodists say yes; Reformed and non-denominational evangelicals holding restrictivism say hearing and believing is necessary (Romans 10). Both say Christ alone saves.
At stake: Whether people who never hear are lost, which shapes how urgent mission seems.

held_by.note: The Catechism says: "Those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel of Christ or his Church, but who nevertheless seek God with a sincere heart, and, moved by grace, try in their actions to do his will as they know it through the dictates of their conscience — those too may achieve eternal salvation" (847).
held_by.citation: Lumen Gentium 16 (1964); Catechism of the Catholic Church, 847

held_by.note: Read from the wider Orthodox emphasis on God's mercy toward the invincibly ignorant rather than from a single conciliar statement.
held_by.citation: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow

held_by.note: Held by a strand within the Communion rather than required by the Articles.
held_by.citation: John Stott and David Edwards, Essentials (1988)

held_by.note: Consistent with Wesley's own doctrine of prevenient grace at work in all people, though Wesley did not draw this precise conclusion himself.
held_by.citation: Clark Pinnock, A Wideness in God's Mercy (1992)

positions.learn_detail: Catholic and Orthodox holders state this as the settled reading of texts like Romans 2, not as a departure from exclusivity of Christ: it is Christ's own saving work, not the sincerity of the seeker, that saves. It should not be described in the terms of a liberal compromise between exclusivism and pluralism.

positions.label: Postmortem opportunity
positions.hold: Those who die without having had a genuine opportunity to hear and respond to the gospel are given that opportunity after death, so that no one is finally condemned for rejecting a message they never encountered.
positions.why: Christ himself is described as proclaiming to spirits in prison, taken as evidence that God provides some who lacked opportunity in this life with a genuine encounter with the gospel beyond it.
positions.vs: Treating death as the fixed and final boundary of opportunity to respond to the gospel for every person without exception.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether people who died without a real chance to hear the gospel are given one after death.
Who: Some evangelical theologians, such as Gabriel Fackre, say yes, citing 1 Peter 3:18–20; most churches teach that a person's response to God is settled at death and read that passage differently, for example as Christ's message through Noah.
At stake: Whether death is the last chance to respond to God, which shapes views of God's fairness.
positions.learn_detail: Associated with theologians such as Gabriel Fackre and, in a more cautious form, with the wider question of what 1 Peter 3-4's proclamation to the spirits in prison actually describes; no tradition registered here confesses it, so held_by is left empty.

sources.label: Gabriel Fackre, in What About Those Who Have Never Heard?

positions.label: Molinist
positions.hold: Explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation, and God, by his knowledge of what every person would freely do under any circumstance, has so ordered the world that everyone who would respond in saving faith if they heard the gospel is in fact brought to hear it.
positions.why: God's knowledge extends to what any free creature would do in any possible circumstance, so God can actualise a world in which the elect are exactly those who hear and no one who would have freely believed the gospel is left to perish for lack of hearing it.
positions.vs: Locating the answer in the content of the salvation offered to the unevangelised, whether through the light of nature or a further postmortem chance, rather than in God's providential ordering of who is brought to hear the gospel in the first place.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether God's knowledge of what each person would freely choose explains why no one who would have believed the gospel fails to hear it.
Who: Supporters such as William Lane Craig, across several traditions, say yes; some Reformed critics reject it because it assumes people can choose either way whatever their circumstances.
At stake: Whether God can be fair to those who never hear while explicit faith in Christ stays necessary.
positions.learn_detail: Associated chiefly with William Lane Craig's argument from transworld damnation: rather than asking what happens to someone who never hears, it asks why God would ever leave someone in circumstances where they would have believed had they heard, and answers that in fact he does not. No tradition registered here confesses Molinism as such; it is held by individual theologians working within several of the traditions above.

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: Unevangelised — people who have never heard the gospel; restrictivism — only those who hear and believe in Christ are saved; inclusivism — Christ alone saves, but his work can reach some who never heard of him; Molinism — God knows what each free person would choose in any situation.
How it developed: Romans 1–2 and 10 are the main texts. Vatican II, a worldwide meeting of Catholic bishops (1962–65), taught that some who never hear the gospel can be saved. The Spanish theologian Luis de Molina (1535–1600) developed Molinism.

sources.label: What About Those Who Have Never Heard? Three Views on the Destiny of the Unevangelized

doctrines.question: How should the teaching and practice of the non-Christian religions be assessed?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition confesses Christ as the unique saviour; the disagreement is over how to regard what the other religions actually teach. Some hold the religions are wholly false, spiritually empty, or actively demonic counterfeits; others hold the religions contain real, if partial and finally insufficient, truth and goodness, the product of God's general revelation and common grace at work among all peoples; and others hold the religions are best read as incomplete anticipations that find their fulfilment in Christ. Judaism, given its unique place in God's revelation, is addressed separately.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the second tier: it shapes the posture and tone of engagement with other religions without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether Paul's appeal to the Athenians' own poets in Acts 17 is a model for finding genuine common ground with other religions, or simply a rhetorical bridge to a message that otherwise owes those religions nothing.

positions.label: False and demonic
positions.hold: The teaching and worship of the non-Christian religions are false and, where they involve the worship of other gods, are in fact offered to demons rather than to God.
positions.why: Paul tells the Corinthians that what pagans sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God, refusing to treat pagan worship as a lesser but still valid approach to the divine.
positions.vs: Treating the teaching of the non-Christian religions as containing real truth and goodness that Christian proclamation can build upon.

positions.label: Rays of truth
positions.hold: The non-Christian religions contain elements of genuine truth and goodness, reflecting the general revelation of God available to all people, but nothing in them is sufficient for salvation apart from Christ.
positions.why: God has not left himself without witness, and what can be known about God is plain to all people because God has shown it to them in creation, so the religions built by those same people can be expected to preserve some genuine, if incomplete, apprehension of that revelation.
positions.vs: Treating the teaching of every non-Christian religion as wholly false with no residue of genuine truth or goodness in it.

held_by.note: The church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions, while proclaiming, and bound to proclaim without fail, Christ as the way, the truth and the life.
held_by.citation: Nostra Aetate 2 (1965)
Lambeth Conference 1988, Resolution 21

held_by.note: Read through the Reformed doctrine of general revelation and common grace.
held_by.citation: Westminster Confession of Faith 1.1; Belgic Confession, Article 2

positions.learn_detail: The Catholic form of this position is Nostra Aetate's language of rays of that truth which enlightens all people; the Reformed and evangelical form is drawn independently from general revelation and common grace rather than from the council. Both converge on the same claim: real truth, insufficient for salvation.

positions.label: Fulfilment
positions.hold: The non-Christian religions represent genuine but incomplete human searching after God, which the gospel of Christ fulfils rather than simply contradicts or replaces.
positions.why: Paul, addressing the Athenians about the god they worshipped without knowing, proclaims that same god to them rather than dismissing their religious searching outright, treating it as something the gospel completes.
positions.vs: Treating the non-Christian religions as having no positive relationship at all to the truth Christ brings, so that the gospel simply displaces rather than fulfils what came before it.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether other religions' search for God is a real but incomplete stage that Christ completes, or holds only scattered truth or none.
Who: Missiologists such as J. N. Farquhar (1913) say Christ completes it; those holding the rays-of-truth view, found in Catholic, Anglican and Reformed teaching, worry this treats religions as steps on one path to Christ.
At stake: Whether missionaries build on what people believe or call them to turn from it.
positions.learn_detail: Associated with missiologists such as J. N. Farquhar's account of Christ as the fulfilment of Hinduism; no tradition registered here confesses this as a formal position, so held_by is left empty.

sources.label: J. N. Farquhar, The Crown of Hinduism

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: General revelation — what God shows everyone through creation and conscience; common grace — God's kindness to all people, not only believers; fulfilment — other religions' search for God is completed in Christ; Nostra Aetate — Vatican II's 1965 statement on other religions.
How it developed: Christians read Paul's Athens sermon (Acts 17) and his warning about sacrifices to demons (1 Corinthians 10) differently. Missionary J. N. Farquhar argued in 1913 that Christ fulfils Hinduism; Nostra Aetate spoke of rays of truth in other religions.

sources.label: Perspectives on the World Christian Movement
sources.citation: Ralph D. Winter and Steven C. Hawthorne, eds., 1981

doctrines.question: How far should the gospel's presentation adapt to a culture's existing religious forms and vocabulary?
doctrines.framing: Paul became all things to all people to win some, adapting his approach to Jews and Gentiles alike without changing the gospel itself. Missiologists describe the resulting spectrum of adaptation using the C1 to C6 scale, running from forms entirely foreign to the local culture through to believers who retain a full religious and cultural identity within their birth community. The disagreement is over how far forms can be adapted or reused before the content of the gospel itself is compromised, and in particular whether believers can remain formally within a non-Christian religious community and identity.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the third tier: it is a live methodological dispute among otherwise cooperating evangelicals rather than a first-order gospel question.

open.todo: Work out where along the C1-C6 spectrum a form becomes so bound up with the theology of another religion that reusing it teaches something false, rather than merely reusing a neutral cultural vessel.

positions.label: Full contextualisation
positions.hold: Cultural and religious forms, including language, dress, music, and social structures, may be freely adapted or reused to carry the gospel, provided the content of the gospel taught through them remains unchanged.
positions.why: Paul became like a Jew to the Jews and like one outside the law to those outside the law, adapting his own conduct and approach to each audience while never altering the gospel he preached to any of them.
positions.vs: Treating a culture's existing forms as so fixed to their prior religious meaning that reusing any of them to carry the gospel is itself a compromise, regardless of what content is actually taught through them.

held_by.note: The Covenant says: "The development of strategies for world evangelization calls for imaginative pioneering methods. Under God, the result will be the rise of churches deeply rooted in Christ and closely related to their culture."
held_by.citation: Lausanne Covenant (1974), Article 10, 'Evangelism and Culture'

held_by.note: Stated as inculturation rather than contextualisation, but the same principle of adapting form while preserving content.
held_by.citation: Ad Gentes 22 (1965)

positions.learn_detail: This position corresponds to the C3-C4 range on the C1-C6 missiological spectrum: significant use of locally meaningful forms and vocabulary, without retaining a formal identity within a non-Christian religious community.

positions.label: Conservative on forms
positions.hold: Some cultural and religious forms are so bound up with the theology of a non-Christian religion that they carry inseparable religious meaning and cannot be safely reused to express the Christian gospel.
positions.why: A form developed to express and reinforce a rival religion's own theology can teach that theology by its very use, whatever content a missionary intends to attach to it, so the safer course is a clean break with such forms rather than an attempt to repurpose them.
positions.vs: Treating any cultural or religious form as a neutral vessel that can be filled with Christian content regardless of the prior theological freight it carries.

held_by.note: A real, self-identified stream within Baptist and independent evangelical missions rather than a confessional position of the Baptist Faith and Message.
held_by.citation: Phil Parshall, criticised in Beyond the Great Divide (2016 debate literature)
Georges Houssney, Engaging Islam (2010)

positions.label: Insider movements
positions.hold: Believers from a Muslim or Hindu background may remain formally within their birth religious community and identity, retaining its outward practices and self-identification, while inwardly following Jesus as Lord and Saviour.
positions.why: Retaining a birth community's social and religious identity removes unnecessary social barriers to faith in Christ and allows a movement to Christ to spread within a family and community network rather than requiring every believer to exit it.
positions.vs: Requiring a convert to a wholly separate visible identity and community, breaking with the religious community and identity into which they were born, before their faith in Christ is recognised as complete.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether someone from a Muslim or Hindu background can follow Jesus while staying inside their birth community and identity, or should join a separate Christian community.
Who: Practitioners, including some non-denominational evangelicals, say yes, citing 1 Corinthians 7:17–20; other evangelical missiologists say it blurs confessing Jesus as Lord and risks syncretism, mixing faiths.
At stake: Whether staying removes needless barriers to faith or hides what conversion means.

held_by.note: A real, self-identified stream within evangelical missions to Muslim-majority contexts, sharply disputed by other evangelical missiologists.
held_by.citation: John Travis, 'The C1 to C6 Spectrum', Evangelical Missions Quarterly (1998)

positions.learn_detail: This corresponds to the C5 category on the C1-C6 spectrum, where believers retain a Muslim or Hindu socio-religious identity; C6, secret believers with no corporate identity at all, is a related but distinct category not itself in dispute in the same way. The critique is stated here in the terms critics themselves use, and the position in the terms its practitioners use, because neither side accepts the other's framing.

sources.label: The C1 to C6 Spectrum
sources.citation: John Travis, Evangelical Missions Quarterly 34, no. 4 (1998)

sources.label: Chrislam or Christ?
sources.citation: Georges Houssney, in Beyond the Great Divide, 2016

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: Contextualisation — adapting how the gospel is presented to fit a culture; C1–C6 spectrum — a six-step scale from C1 (forms wholly foreign to the local culture) to C6 (secret believers with no public community); insider movement — believers who keep a Muslim or Hindu identity while following Jesus (C5).
How it developed: The word first appeared in a 1972 report of the Theological Education Fund, which supported training church leaders. Missionary John Travis published the C1–C6 scale in 1998, for Muslim settings; it became the standard way to compare adaptation.

sources.label: The C1 to C6 Spectrum
sources.citation: John Travis, Evangelical Missions Quarterly 34, no. 4 (1998)

non-denominational.hold: Most non-denominational evangelical missions favour full contextualisation of forms while keeping the gospel's content unchanged; a minority stream working in Muslim-majority contexts practises insider-movement methods, which other evangelicals in the same stream sharply dispute.
non-denominational.note: This is a live methodological dispute within the stream itself, not a settled position: insider-movement practitioners and their evangelical critics both identify as non-denominational evangelicals.
non-denominational.citation: Lausanne Covenant (1974), Article 10, contrasted with John Travis, 'The C1 to C6 Spectrum', Evangelical Missions Quarterly (1998)

doctrines.question: Should the church direct evangelistic effort toward Jewish people, and on what understanding of Israel's covenant with God?
doctrines.framing: This doctrine asks a missiological question distinct from how Israel and the church relate in the unfolding of covenant history: whether, and how, the church should evangelise Jewish people specifically. The disagreement is over whether Jewish people are included in the Great Commission without distinction from any other people, whether their standing in God's covenant with Israel means explicit faith in Christ is not required of them as it is of others, or whether the church, while never denying that salvation is from Christ, should neither conduct nor support an institutional mission targeted at Jews specifically. This history includes real and grave persecution of Jewish people carried out in the church's name, and the entries below describe positions rather than adjudicate between them.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places this at the third tier: a matter of real and careful disagreement among traditions that otherwise share the same gospel, not a first-order test of orthodoxy.

open.todo: Work out how Romans 11:29's statement that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable bears on whether Jewish people need to hear and believe the gospel as anyone else does, and decide whether the Catholic position after Nostra Aetate on institutional mission is the right balance or an unstable one.

positions.label: No distinction
positions.hold: The Great Commission includes Jewish people without any distinction from other peoples, so the church is to proclaim the gospel to Jewish people just as it does to everyone else, in fulfilment rather than betrayal of God's covenant with Israel.
positions.why: The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek, naming Jewish people as the first, not the excluded, recipients of that same gospel.
positions.vs: Treating Jewish people as a people for whom explicit faith in Christ is not required, or as a people the church should decline to evangelise as it evangelises others.

held_by.citation: Westminster Confession of Faith 10.4

positions.learn_detail: Paul's own stated longing for the salvation of his fellow Israelites, and his description of the gospel as for the Jew first, are read here as ruling out any exemption of Jewish people from ordinary gospel proclamation.

positions.label: Dual covenant
positions.hold: Jewish people stand in God's covenant with Israel, which God has not revoked, and remain in a right relationship with God through that covenant without requiring explicit faith in Jesus Christ.
positions.why: God's gifts and his call to Israel are irrevocable, so the covenant God made with Israel is read as still standing on its own terms and sufficient for that people's relationship with God, apart from faith in Christ.
positions.vs: Holding that explicit faith in Jesus Christ is necessary for salvation without exception, including for Jewish people despite their covenant with God.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether Jewish people stay in right relationship with God through his covenant with Israel, without faith in Jesus.
Who: Some mainline Protestant statements say yes, citing Romans 11:29; churches holding that the Great Commission includes Jewish people, such as many Reformed, say all need faith in Christ. No creed settles it.
At stake: One side fears denying that Christ is necessary for everyone; the other fears denying that God keeps his promises to Israel.
positions.learn_detail: Argued chiefly from Romans 11:29 and adopted as an official or semi-official position by some mainline Protestant denominational statements on relations with Judaism; no tradition registered in this corpus holds it, so held_by is left empty rather than assigned by inference.

positions.label: No institutional mission
positions.hold: The church neither conducts nor supports any institutional mission specifically directed at Jews, while continuing to bear witness to faith in Jesus Christ and never denying that salvation flows from Christ alone.
positions.why: God's gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable, and the church's own reflection on its unique bond with the Jewish people leads it to reject a programme of institutional mission aimed specifically at Jews, without this meaning it ceases to believe or proclaim that salvation is from Christ.
positions.vs: Directing an institutional missionary programme specifically at Jewish people in the same way the church directs mission toward other, non-covenanted peoples.
positions.orthodoxy_note:
Disputed: Whether the church should run organised missions aimed at Jewish people, as it does for other peoples.
Who: The Catholic Church, in a 2015 Vatican document, neither conducts nor supports such a mission, while teaching salvation is from Christ; many evangelical churches say Jewish people should be evangelised like everyone else.
At stake: Whether this honours God's lasting bond with Israel, or weakens the call to share the gospel with all.

held_by.note: Verbatim, §40: "In concrete terms this means that the Catholic Church neither conducts nor supports any specific institutional mission work directed towards Jews. ... Christians are nonetheless called to bear witness to their faith in Jesus Christ also to Jews, although they should do so in a humble and sensitive manner, acknowledging that Jews are bearers of God's Word." The document states its own status in its preface: "The text is not a magisterial document or doctrinal teaching of the Catholic Church, but is a reflection prepared by the Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews." Nostra Aetate 4 (1965), the binding conciliar text, does not itself address institutional mission to Jews at all; the specific no-institutional-mission position rests only on this later, explicitly non-magisterial reflection.
held_by.citation: Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, "The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable" (10 December 2015), §40

positions.learn_detail: This position must be stated with precision: it is a specific judgment about institutional missionary programmes aimed at Jews, made explicit in the 2015 document The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable from the Vatican's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, and it explicitly does not deny that Jesus Christ is the way, the truth and the life, nor that salvation comes through him.

sources.label: The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable
sources.citation: Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, 10 December 2015, §40

doctrines.learn_note:
Key terms: Great Commission — Jesus' command to take the gospel to all nations (Matthew 28:19–20); covenant — a binding promise God made to a people; dual covenant — Jewish people stay right with God through his covenant with Israel, without faith in Jesus.
How it developed: Christianity began as a Jewish movement, and Paul wrestled with Israel's place in Romans 9–11. Jewish people long suffered persecution, including forced conversion, by Christians. Vatican II (1965) condemned hatred of Jews; a 2015 Vatican document said the Catholic Church conducts no mission aimed at Jews.

sources.label: The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable
sources.citation: Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, 10 December 2015
